vim-word-forward.title: Where does `w` land?
vim-word-forward.description:
Model Vim's `w` motion (jump to the start of the next *word*) on a single line.

Characters fall into three classes:

| class | characters |
|---|---|
| blank | space and tab |
| keyword | `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, `_` |
| punctuation | every other character |

A **word** is a maximal run of keyword characters *or* a maximal run of punctuation characters.
So `foo.bar()` contains four words: `foo`, `.`, `bar`, `()`.

One press of `w` from column `col`:

1. if the cursor is on a non-blank, skip to the end of the run it is in;
2. skip any blanks;
3. land on the first character of the next word.

This model has only one line: if there is no next word, the cursor moves to the **last character of the
line** (index `len(line) - 1`). On an empty line the answer is always `0`.

Write `wordForward(line, col, count)` returning the column after pressing `w` `count` times
(`count >= 1`, `0 <= col < len(line)` unless the line is empty).

**Example:** `line = "total += price*qty"`, `col = 0`, `count = 1` → `6` (the `+`)

**Example:** same line, `col = 0`, `count = 3` → `14` (the `*`)
vim-word-forward.starter:
def wordForward(line: str, col: int, count: int) -> int:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Motions* lesson (word-wise movement). String indexing and `while` loops.
guide.intuition: `w` does not look for spaces; it looks for a **change of character class**. Classify every character as blank, keyword or punctuation, then walk right: leave the run you are standing in, cross any blanks, and stop on the first non-blank you meet.
hints: Write a helper `cls(ch)` that returns 0, 1 or 2. Everything else is two `while` loops.
The first loop only runs when the cursor starts on a non-blank; starting on a blank you just skip blanks.
If the index runs off the end of the line there was no next word: return `len(line) - 1` immediately.
guide.brute_force: Split the line into tokens with a regular expression such as `\w+|[^\w\s]+`, record each token's start column, and pick the first start greater than `col`, `count` times. It works but hides the class-change idea and is easy to get wrong for blanks.
guide.approach:
Repeat `count` times: read the class at `col`; if it is non-blank advance while the class stays the same; then advance while the class is blank; if you fell off the end return the last column, otherwise that index is the new `col`.

**Dry run** on `foo.bar()` from 0 with count 3: class at 0 is keyword, skip `foo` → index 3 (`.`), no blanks, col = 3. Class punctuation, skip `.` → 4 (`b`), col = 4. Class keyword, skip `bar` → 7 (`(`), col = 7. Answer 7.
guide.complexity: Time O(count + n) in practice (each press only moves right; once the end is reached we return), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Treating `foo.bar` as one word: that is `W`, not `w`.
- Returning `len(line)` instead of `len(line) - 1` when no word follows; the Normal-mode cursor can never sit past the last character.
- Forgetting the empty line.
- An underscore is a keyword character, so `snake_case` is one word.
guide.follow_up: Add `W`, `b` and `e` (next problem), then a multi-line version where `w` wraps to the next line.

vim-word-motions.title: Replay a string of w / b / e / W / B / E
vim-word-motions.description:
Extend the word model to all six word motions and replay a sequence of them on one line.

Character classes for the lowercase motions are **blank** (space, tab), **keyword** (`A-Za-z0-9_`) and
**punctuation** (anything else). For the uppercase motions there are only two classes: blank and non-blank, so
a WORD is any run of non-blank characters.

| key | rule (single-line model) |
|---|---|
| `w` / `W` | leave the current run if on a non-blank, skip blanks, land on the first character of the next run. No next run → last character of the line. |
| `e` / `E` | step one character right, skip blanks, then go to the **last** character of the run you are in. Nothing but blanks (or nothing) to the right → last character of the line. |
| `b` / `B` | step one character left, skip blanks leftwards, then go to the **first** character of the run you are in. Nothing but blanks (or nothing) to the left → column 0. |

On an empty line every motion leaves the cursor at column 0.

Write `wordMotions(line, col, keys)` where `keys` contains only the characters `wbeWBE`; return the final column.

**Example:** `line = "user.name = input()"`, `col = 0`, `keys = "e"` → `3`

**Example:** same line, `col = 0`, `keys = "WW"` → `12`

**Example:** same line, `col = 12`, `keys = "bb"` → `5`
vim-word-motions.starter:
def wordMotions(line: str, col: int, keys: str) -> int:
    pass

guide.prereqs: `vim-word-forward`. The difference between a word and a WORD from the *Motions* lesson.
guide.intuition: All six motions are the same three steps in a different order: *get off where you are*, *cross the blanks*, *slide to an edge of the run*. `e` and `b` must move at least one character first, otherwise pressing `e` at the end of a word would never go anywhere.
hints: Make the classifier take a flag: with the flag set, every non-blank is class 1.
`e`: `i += 1`, skip blanks to the right, then extend right while the next character has the same class.
`b` is the mirror image of `e`: `i -= 1`, skip blanks to the left, extend left while the previous character has the same class.
guide.brute_force: Tokenise the line into runs with their start and end columns (once for words, once for WORDs) and for each key scan the token list for the first start greater than the cursor (`w`), first end greater than the cursor (`e`) or last start smaller than the cursor (`b`). O(keys × tokens).
guide.approach:
Loop over the keys. Decide `big = key.isupper()`. Apply the rule for the lower-cased key using the class function.

**Dry run** `user.name = input()` from 12 with `bb`: first `b`: step to 11 (blank), skip blanks left to 10 (`=`), run `=` starts at 10 → col 10. Second `b`: step to 9 (blank), skip to 8 (`e`), slide left through `name` to 5 → col 5.
guide.complexity: O(len(keys) × n) worst case, O(1) extra space.
guide.pitfalls:
- Forgetting the mandatory first step for `e`/`b`: the cursor then gets stuck on a word edge.
- Using the three-class classifier for the uppercase motions.
- `e` on trailing blanks and `b` on leading blanks have no target: clamp to the last column or column 0.
- Off-by-one when sliding to the edge: test the *neighbour's* class, not the current one.
guide.follow_up: Add `ge`/`gE` (backward to end of word) and counts such as `3w`.

vim-line-anchors.title: Line anchors: 0, ^, $ and g_
vim-line-anchors.description:
Four Normal-mode motions jump to a fixed place on the current line, regardless of where the cursor was:

| key | lands on |
|---|---|
| `0` | column 0 |
| `^` | the first non-blank character; on a line made only of blanks, the **last** character |
| `$` | the last character |
| `g_` | the last non-blank character; on a line made only of blanks, column 0 |

Blanks are spaces and tabs. On an empty line all four return `0`.

Write `lineAnchor(line, key)` returning the 0-based column.

**Example:** `line = "    return x  "`, `key = "^"` → `4`

**Example:** same line, `key = "g_"` → `11`; `key = "$"` → `13`
vim-line-anchors.starter:
def lineAnchor(line: str, key: str) -> int:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Motions* lesson. Basic string scanning.
guide.intuition: These are absolute motions: the starting column is irrelevant. The only thinking required is what happens when the thing being looked for (a non-blank) does not exist.
hints: Handle the empty line first; then `0` and `$` are one-liners.
`^` scans from the left for the first character that is not a space or tab.
When the whole line is blank, `^` ends on the last column but `g_` ends on column 0. They are not symmetric.
guide.brute_force: There is nothing slower than a linear scan here; the naive approach is the right one.
guide.approach:
Branch on the key. For `^` scan left to right, for `g_` scan right to left, each with a fallback.

**Dry run** on `····return x··` (dots are spaces, length 14): `^` finds `r` at 4; `g_` scans back from 13, 12 (blanks) to 11 (`x`); `$` is 13.
guide.pitfalls:
- `len(line) - len(line.lstrip())` gives `len(line)` on an all-blank line, which is past the end.
- `$` is `len - 1`, not `len`: in Normal mode the cursor sits *on* a character.
- Tabs are blanks too.
guide.follow_up: As operator targets these behave differently: `d$` includes the last character, while `d0` and `d^` exclude the character under the cursor. Try modelling that.

vim-find-char.title: f, t, F, T and their repeats ; and ,
vim-find-char.description:
Simulate Vim's character-search motions on one line. `keys` is a string made of these commands:

| command | meaning |
|---|---|
| `f{c}` | move **onto** the nearest `c` strictly right of the cursor |
| `F{c}` | move **onto** the nearest `c` strictly left of the cursor |
| `t{c}` | find the nearest `c` strictly right of the cursor and stop **one column before** it |
| `T{c}` | find the nearest `c` strictly left of the cursor and stop **one column after** it |
| `;` | repeat the most recent `f/F/t/T` in the same direction |
| `,` | repeat it in the opposite direction (`f`↔`F`, `t`↔`T`) |

Rules:

- The character after `f`, `F`, `t` or `T` is always taken literally, even if it is `;`, `,` or a letter such as `f`.
- If the target is not found the cursor does not move (the command is still remembered for `;` and `,`).
- `;` and `,` never change which search is remembered. Before any search has been made they do nothing.
- **Repeat rule for t/T:** when a `t`-style search is run through `;` or `,`, the character directly next to the
  cursor in the search direction is skipped, so that the repeat makes progress instead of finding the same
  occurrence again. A freshly typed `t{c}` or `T{c}` does *not* skip: if the neighbour is `c`, the cursor stays put.

Write `findChar(line, col, keys)` returning the final column.

**Example:** `line = "a, b, c, d"`, `col = 0`, `keys = "f,;"` → `4`

**Example:** same line, `col = 0`, `keys = "t,;;"` → `6`

**Example:** same line, `col = 9`, `keys = "F,,"` → `7` (`F,` goes to 7, then `,` searches right for a comma: none, so stay)
vim-find-char.starter:
def findChar(line: str, col: int, keys: str) -> int:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Motions* lesson (find by character). `str.find` / `str.rfind` with start and end bounds.
guide.intuition: There are really two commands (search right, search left) and one modifier (stop on the target or next to it). `;` and `,` replay a remembered pair *(kind, char)*; `,` flips the direction for one replay only. The single subtle rule is the skip that keeps a repeated `t` from getting stuck.
hints: Parse two characters at a time for `f/F/t/T`, one at a time for `;` and `,`.
Write one helper `run(kind, ch, col, repeat)`; `,` just calls it with the flipped kind.
For a repeated `t`, start searching at `col + 2`; for a repeated `T`, search the slice `[0, col - 1)`.
guide.brute_force: Scan character by character with explicit loops instead of `find`/`rfind`. Same complexity, more places for an off-by-one.
guide.approach:
Keep `last = (kind, char)`. For each command compute the search window, look for the character, and convert the hit to a landing column (`idx`, `idx - 1` or `idx + 1`).

**Dry run** `a, b, c, d` from 0 with `t,;;`: `t,` finds the comma at 1, lands on 0. `;` repeats with the skip: search from column 2, comma at 4, land on 3. `;` again: search from 5, comma at 7, land on 6.
guide.pitfalls:
- Treating `;` after `f` as a command: in `f;` the semicolon is the target.
- Letting `,` overwrite the remembered direction; after `f,` then `,` then `;`, the `;` still searches right.
- A repeated `t` without the skip finds the same occurrence forever.
- `rfind(ch, 0, end)` with a negative `end` counts from the right; clamp it to 0.
guide.follow_up: Add counts (`2f,`) and use the result as an operator target: `dt,` deletes up to but not including the comma, `df,` includes it.

vim-text-object-word.title: Resolve iw and aw
vim-text-object-word.description:
Text objects select a region *around the cursor*, wherever in the region the cursor happens to be.
Resolve the two word objects on a single line and return the selection as a half-open range `[start, end)`.

Character classes: **blank** (space, tab), **keyword** (`A-Za-z0-9_`), **punctuation** (everything else).
A *run* is a maximal stretch of characters of one class.

**`iw` (inner word)** selects the run under the cursor, whatever its class. On a run of blanks, `iw`
selects those blanks.

**`aw` (a word)**:

- cursor on a non-blank run: the run **plus the blanks that follow it**. If no blanks follow (the run is
  followed by another non-blank run or by the end of the line), take the blanks **before** it instead. If
  there are none on either side, just the run.
- cursor on a blank run: the blanks **plus the non-blank run that follows**. If nothing follows, just the blanks.

An empty line yields `[0, 0]`.

Write `wordObject(line, col, obj)` with `obj` equal to `"iw"` or `"aw"`.

**Example:** `line = "let total = 0"`, `col = 6`, `obj = "iw"` → `[4, 9]`

**Example:** same line, `col = 6`, `obj = "aw"` → `[4, 10]` (deleting it leaves `let = 0`)

**Example:** `line = "drop the last"`, `col = 10`, `obj = "aw"` → `[8, 13]` (no blanks after, so take the one before)
vim-text-object-word.starter:
def wordObject(line: str, col: int, obj: str) -> List[int]:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Text objects* lesson. `vim-word-forward` for the character classes.
guide.intuition: Find the run under the cursor by growing left and right while the class stays the same: that is `iw`. `aw` exists so that deleting a word leaves tidy spacing, so it grabs one neighbouring stretch of blanks, preferring the trailing one.
hints: Write `run(i)` returning the half-open bounds of the run containing index `i`; you will call it up to twice.
For `aw` on a non-blank: check `line[e]` first (trailing blanks), then `line[s-1]` (leading blanks).
For `aw` on blanks, the second call is `run(e)` to swallow the following word.
guide.brute_force: Tokenise the whole line into runs, find the one containing the cursor, and look at its neighbours in the token list. O(n) as well, but builds a list you do not need.
guide.approach:
Compute `(s, e) = run(col)`. Return it for `iw`. For `aw` extend by exactly one neighbouring run according to the rules.

**Dry run** `drop the last`, col 10, `aw`: run is `last` = [9, 13). `e == n`, so no trailing blanks. `line[8]` is a blank; its run is [8, 9). Result [8, 13).
guide.pitfalls:
- Returning an inclusive end: the range is half-open.
- Taking both leading *and* trailing blanks; `aw` takes one side only.
- Forgetting that punctuation forms its own run: in `obj.method`, `iw` on the dot is just the dot.
- `aw` at the end of a line must fall back to the leading blanks, otherwise `daw` on the last word would leave trailing whitespace.
guide.follow_up: Implement `iW`/`aW`, and `daw` followed by `.` to delete several words in a row.

vim-text-object-quote.title: Resolve i" and a"
vim-text-object-quote.description:
Resolve the quote text objects on one line. `obj` is `i"`, `a"`, `i'` or `a'`; the second character is the quote
character `q`. There are no escaped quotes in this model. Return a half-open range `[start, end)`, or `[-1, -1]`
when no quoted string can be found.

**Step 1: find the pair of quotes** (`open`, `close` are their columns):

- If the character under the cursor is `q`: count the `q` characters from the start of the line up to and
  including the cursor. An **odd** count means the cursor is on an opening quote; `close` is the next `q` to the
  right. An **even** count means it is on a closing quote; `open` is the previous `q` to the left.
- Otherwise, if there is a `q` somewhere left of the cursor: `open` is the nearest one on the left and `close`
  the nearest one on the right.
- Otherwise (no `q` to the left): look ahead. `open` is the first `q` right of the cursor and `close` the next
  `q` after that. This is what lets `ci"` work from the start of a line.
- If the needed partner does not exist, return `[-1, -1]`.

**Step 2: choose the range**

- `i` → `[open + 1, close)` (may be empty)
- `a` → both quotes, **plus the blanks (spaces/tabs) immediately after the closing quote**; if there are none,
  plus the blanks immediately before the opening quote.

**Example:** `line = 'msg = "hi there" + name'`, `col = 9`, `obj = 'i"'` → `[7, 15]`

**Example:** same line, `col = 0`, `obj = 'a"'` → `[6, 17]` (looked ahead; trailing space included)

**Example:** `line = "no quotes here"`, `col = 3`, `obj = 'i"'` → `[-1, -1]`
vim-text-object-quote.starter:
def quoteObject(line: str, col: int, obj: str) -> List[int]:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Text objects* lesson (delimited objects). `str.find`, `str.rfind`, `str.count` with bounds.
guide.intuition: Quotes are harder than brackets because the opening and closing characters are identical. Vim resolves the ambiguity with a parity count when the cursor is *on* a quote, and with nearest neighbours otherwise. The look-ahead case is a convenience so you do not have to move onto the string first.
hints: Split into the two cases *cursor on q* and *cursor not on q* before writing any search.
`line.count(q, 0, col + 1) % 2` tells you opening versus closing.
For `a`: extend right over blanks; only if you did not move, extend left over blanks.
guide.brute_force: Pair the quotes two by two from the start of the line and return the first pair that ends at or after the cursor. That matches Vim in the common cases but gives a different answer when the cursor sits *between* two strings, where this model uses the nearest quote on each side.
guide.approach:
Find `open`/`close` using the three-way rule, bail out with `[-1, -1]` if either is missing, then build the range.

**Dry run** `msg = "hi there" + name`, col 0, `a"`: cursor is not on a quote and nothing lies to its left, so look ahead: open = 6, close = 15. Range starts as [6, 16); column 16 is a space, extend to 17. Result [6, 17).
guide.pitfalls:
- Pairing quotes from the start of the line in every case.
- Forgetting the look-ahead when the cursor is before the first quote.
- `a"` takes trailing blanks *or* leading blanks, never both.
- An empty string `""` gives an empty inner range, not a failure.
guide.follow_up: Support backslash-escaped quotes (Vim honours the `quoteescape` option), and the backtick object.

vim-text-object-bracket.title: Resolve i( a( i[ a[ i{ a{
vim-text-object-bracket.description:
Resolve bracket text objects on one line. `obj` is two characters: `i` or `a`, followed by one of

| second character | pair |
|---|---|
| `(` `)` or `b` | `( )` |
| `[` or `]` | `[ ]` |
| `{` `}` or `B` | `{ }` |

Only the chosen pair type matters; other bracket types are ordinary characters.

**Finding the pair.** The object is the innermost pair that *encloses* the cursor, where a cursor sitting on
either bracket of a pair counts as enclosed by that pair:

- cursor on an opening bracket → that is `open`;
- cursor on a closing bracket → `open` is its matching opener (scan left, tracking nesting depth);
- otherwise scan left from the cursor for the first *unmatched* opener.

Then `close` is the bracket matching `open` (scan right, tracking depth). If either scan fails, return `[-1, -1]`.
Unlike the quote objects, bracket objects in this model never look ahead.

**Range** (half-open): `i` → `[open + 1, close)`, `a` → `[open, close + 1)`.

Write `bracketObject(line, col, obj)`.

**Example:** `line = "run(a, f(b), c)"`, `col = 5`, `obj = "i("` → `[4, 14]`

**Example:** same line, `col = 9`, `obj = "a)"` → `[8, 11]`

**Example:** same line, `col = 1`, `obj = "ib"` → `[-1, -1]`
vim-text-object-bracket.starter:
def bracketObject(line: str, col: int, obj: str) -> List[int]:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Text objects* lesson. Bracket matching with a depth counter (the classic valid-parentheses idea).
guide.intuition: Walk left counting closers you pass; an opener cancels one pending closer, and the first opener seen with nothing pending is the one that encloses the cursor. From there walk right with the mirror-image counter to find its partner.
hints: Map the second character of `obj` to an `(open, close)` pair first; `b` and `B` are aliases.
Special-case the cursor sitting on the opener. A cursor on the closer needs no special case if your left scan starts at `col - 1`.
The right scan must start at `open + 1`, not at the cursor, or nested pairs between them will be miscounted.
guide.brute_force: Precompute all matching pairs with a stack in one pass, then choose the pair with the largest `open` satisfying `open <= col <= close`. O(n) time and O(n) space; perfectly acceptable.
guide.approach:
Left scan for `open`, right scan for `close`, then slice.

**Dry run** `run(a, f(b), c)`, col 5, `i(`: `line[5]` is a comma. Scan left: 4 `a`, 3 `(` with depth 0 → open = 3. Scan right from 4: `(` at 8 → depth 1, `)` at 10 → depth 0, `)` at 14 with depth 0 → close = 14. Inner range [4, 14).
guide.pitfalls:
- `rfind`/`find` for the nearest brackets ignores nesting and breaks on `f(g(x), y)`.
- Forgetting that the cursor may be on the opener itself.
- Counting other bracket types: `a(b]c)` is fine for `i(`.
- Empty pairs `()` produce an empty inner range.
guide.follow_up: Add the `<`/`>` pair and multi-line buffers; then compare with `%`, which jumps between the same partners.

vim-text-object-tag.title: Resolve it and at
vim-text-object-tag.description:
Resolve the tag text objects on one line of markup. **Input guarantees.** The line contains opening tags `` or `` and closing tags ``, where `name` matches `[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9-]*`. There are no self-closing tags, no comments, and `<` / `>` appear only as tag delimiters. Tags are properly nested and every opening tag has its closing tag. An **element** runs from the `<` of its opening tag to the `>` of its closing tag. The object refers to the **innermost element that contains the cursor column** (a cursor anywhere on the opening or closing tag is inside that element). Return a half-open range `[start, end)`: - `it` → the content between the opening tag's `>` and the closing tag's `<` (may be empty); - `at` → the whole element, both tags included. If the cursor is not inside any element, return `[-1, -1]`. Write `tagObject(line, col, obj)`. **Example:** `line = '
  • Docs now
    • '`, `col = 18`, `obj = "it"` → `[17, 21]` (`Docs`) **Example:** same line, `col = 27`, `obj = "it"` → `[4, 29]` **Example:** same line, `col = 5`, `obj = "at"` → `[4, 25]`

hints: One regular expression can find both kinds of tag; a captured `/` tells them apart.
Store `(start_of_open_tag, end_of_open_tag)` on the stack so both `it` and `at` can be answered later.
Containment test: `open_start <= col < close_end`. Keep the candidate with the largest `open_start`.

Stack pass over the tags; on each closer, pop, test containment and update the best candidate. **Dry run** `

  • ` pushed (0, 4); `` pushed (4, 17); `` at [21, 25) pops the anchor, 4 <= 27 < 25 is false; `

- Using the nearest `>` on the left and `</` on the right ignores nesting and siblings.

vim-delete-motion.title: Apply d{motion} to a line
vim-delete-motion.description:
An operator acts on the text between the cursor and wherever the motion would take it. Apply one delete
command to a single line and report the new line and the new cursor column.

Character classes are **blank** (space, tab), **keyword** (`A-Za-z0-9_`) and **punctuation** (the rest); a word
is a maximal run of keyword characters or of punctuation characters.

| `cmd` | text removed (columns, `n = len(line)`) |
|---|---|
| `x` | the character under the cursor |
| `d$` | from the cursor to the end of the line, inclusive |
| `d0` | from column 0 up to, but **not** including, the cursor |
| `dw` | from the cursor up to, not including, the start of the next word (leave the current run if on a non-blank, then skip blanks). If there is no next word, everything to the end of the line. |
| `de` | from the cursor through the end of the word found by: step right one character, skip blanks, slide to the last character of that run. If only blanks (or nothing) lie to the right, everything to the end of the line. |
| `db` | from the start of the word found by stepping left one character, skipping blanks leftwards and sliding to the first character of that run (column 0 if there is none) up to, not including, the cursor |
| `dt{c}` | from the cursor up to, not including, the next `c` strictly right of the cursor |
| `df{c}` | the same but including that `c` |

If the target of `dt`/`df` does not exist, nothing changes and the cursor stays where it was.

**Cursor afterwards:** the column where the deleted text started, clamped so that it is still on a character
(`min(start, len(new_line) - 1)`, and never below 0). On an empty line every command returns `["", 0]`.

Write `applyDelete(line, col, cmd)` returning `[new_line, new_col]`.

**Example:** `line = "retry_count = limit + 1"`, `col = 0`, `cmd = "dw"` → `["= limit + 1", 0]`

**Example:** same line, `col = 14`, `cmd = "d$"` → `["retry_count = ", 13]`

**Example:** `line = "open(path, mode)"`, `col = 5`, `cmd = "dt,"` → `["open(, mode)", 5]`

def applyDelete(line: str, col: int, cmd: str) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Normal mode grammar* lesson (operator + motion), `vim-word-motions` and `vim-find-char`.
guide.intuition: Every command reduces to a half-open slice `[s, e)` of the line to cut out. The motion decides one end, the cursor is the other. The only real knowledge is which motions are **exclusive** (`w`, `b`, `0`, `t`: the destination character survives) and which are **inclusive** (`e`, `$`, `f`: it is deleted too).
hints: Start with `s = e = col` and let each command move exactly one of the two ends.
Reuse the word-motion loops, but for `dw` let the index run to `n` instead of clamping to `n - 1`.
Inclusive motions add one to the end index: `de` ends at `i + 1`, `df` at `idx + 1`.
guide.brute_force: Compute the motion's landing column with a motion function, then post-process: add one for inclusive motions and special-case `dw` at the end of the line. Equivalent, but the special case is easy to forget because the motion function clamps to the last character.
guide.approach:
Dispatch on `cmd`, compute `[s, e)`, splice, clamp the cursor.

**Dry run** `retry_count = limit + 1`, col 14 (`l`), `db`: step to 13 (blank), skip blanks to 12 (`=`), the run `=` starts at 12, so `s = 12`, `e = 14`. Result `retry_count limit + 1`, cursor 12.
guide.complexity: O(n) time and space (building the new string).
guide.pitfalls:
- Mixing up inclusive and exclusive: `dt,` keeps the comma, `df,` removes it.
- `dw` on the last word must delete to the end of the line.
- After `d$` the cursor cannot stay at `col`; that column no longer exists.
- A failed `dt`/`df` is a no-op, not a delete-to-end.
guide.follow_up: Add counts (`d2w`, `2dw`, `d3f,`) and notice that `d2w` and `2dw` give the same result.

vim-change-command.title: Apply a change command and type the replacement
vim-change-command.description:
A change command deletes a region, enters Insert mode, and whatever is typed before `<Esc>` replaces the region.
Simulate `cmd`, then typing `text`, then `<Esc>`, on a single line.

| `cmd` | region replaced (half-open, `n = len(line)`) |
|---|---|
| `cc` | the whole line `[0, n)` (this model ignores auto-indent) |
| `C` | `[col, n)` |
| `s` | the character under the cursor (nothing on an empty line) |
| `cw` | from the cursor to the end of the **run** it is in (runs are keyword `A-Za-z0-9_`, punctuation, or blank). Note the difference from `dw`: the blanks after a word are **kept**. On a blank, the rest of that run of blanks is replaced. |
| `ct{c}` / `cf{c}` | from the cursor up to (excluding / including) the next `c` strictly to the right |
| `ci"` / `ci'` | the inside of a quoted string, located exactly as in *Resolve i" and a"*: on a quote use the parity of the count of quotes up to the cursor; otherwise nearest quote on each side; with no quote on the left, look ahead to the first pair |
| `ci(` `ci)` `ci[` `ci]` `ci{` `ci}` | the inside of the innermost enclosing pair, located exactly as in *Resolve i( a( …* (cursor on a bracket counts as inside; no look-ahead) |

If the region cannot be found (missing character, quote or bracket), nothing happens: return `[line, col]`.

**Cursor afterwards.** `<Esc>` moves the cursor one column left of the insertion point, so it rests on the last
character typed: `start + len(text) - 1`. If `text` is empty it is `start - 1`. Never below 0.

Write `applyChange(line, col, cmd, text)` returning `[new_line, new_col]`.

**Example:** `line = 'log.info("started")'`, `col = 0`, `cmd = 'ci"'`, `text = "ready"` → `['log.info("ready")', 14]`

**Example:** `line = "timeout = 30  # seconds"`, `col = 0`, `cmd = "cw"`, `text = "deadline"` → `["deadline = 30  # seconds", 7]`

**Example:** `line = "sum(xs[1:], start)"`, `col = 8`, `cmd = "ci("`, `text = ""` → `["sum()", 3]`
vim-change-command.starter:
def applyChange(line: str, col: int, cmd: str, text: str) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: `vim-delete-motion`, `vim-text-object-quote`, `vim-text-object-bracket`, and the *Dot formula* lesson (why `c` commands make good repeatable changes).
guide.intuition: `c` is `d` followed by an insert, with one twist: `cw` stops at the end of the word instead of swallowing the following blanks, because you are about to type a replacement word and want the spacing to survive. After `<Esc>` the cursor steps back onto the last typed character.
hints: Compute a half-open region for each command; `None` means the command failed.
Copy the quote and bracket resolvers from the text-object problems and return only the *inner* range.
The final column is `start + len(text) - 1`, or `start - 1` for empty text, floored at 0.
guide.brute_force: Handle every command with its own splice and cursor formula. It works, but duplicating the splice and the `<Esc>` rule a dozen times invites inconsistent off-by-ones.
guide.approach:
One dispatcher yields `(s, e)` or `None`; one tail builds `line[:s] + text + line[e:]` and the cursor.

**Dry run** `sum(xs[1:], start)`, col 8 (`:`), `ci(`, empty text: scanning left from 7 meets `[` (not a paren, ignored) and the `(` at 3 with depth 0, so open = 3; scanning right the first `)` at depth 0 is at 17. Region [4, 17). New line `sum()`; cursor = 4 - 1 = 3.
guide.pitfalls:
- Giving `cw` the range of `dw`: the blank after the word must stay.
- Leaving the cursor after the inserted text: `<Esc>` moves it left by one.
- Inserting `text` when the region was not found; a failed command changes nothing.
- For `ci(` only parentheses count towards nesting depth.
guide.follow_up: Make the function return a closure that replays the same change at another column: that is the dot command.

vim-golf-score.title: Count keystrokes (VimGolf scoring)
vim-golf-score.description:
Editing plans are written in Vim's key notation, where special keys appear in angle brackets. VimGolf-style
scoring charges **one point per key press**, and a chord such as Ctrl-R is one press.

Tokenise `keys` from left to right:

- A **special key** is `<NAME>` where `NAME` is one of `Esc`, `CR`, `Enter`, `Return`, `Tab`, `BS`, `Del`,
  `Space`, `lt`, `Bar`, `Up`, `Down`, `Left`, `Right`, `Home`, `End`, or `F` followed by one or two digits.
  It counts as **1**.
- A **chord** is `<` + one or more modifier prefixes (`C-`, `S-`, `A-`, `M-`) + either a single character or one
  of the names above + `>`; for example `<C-r>`, `<C-S-Tab>`, `<A-CR>`. It counts as **1**.
- Names and modifiers are case-insensitive (`<esc>`, `<c-R>` are fine).
- Anything else is a single ordinary key worth **1**, including a `<` that does not start a valid special key
  (so `<<` is two keys, and `<foo>` is five).

Write `golfScore(keys)` returning the total.

**Example:** `"ciwtotal<Esc>"` → `9` (`c`, `i`, `w`, five letters, `<Esc>`)

**Example:** `":%s/a/b/g<CR>"` → `10`

**Example:** `"A;<Esc>j."` → `5`
vim-golf-score.solution:
import re

_NAME = r"(?:Esc|CR|Enter|Return|Tab|BS|Del|Space|lt|Bar|Up|Down|Left|Right|Home|End|F[0-9]{1,2})"
_KEY = re.compile(r"<(?:(?:[CSAM]-)+(?:" + _NAME + r"|.)|" + _NAME + r")>", re.I | re.S)

def golfScore(keys):
    i = 0
    total = 0
    while i < len(keys):
        m = _KEY.match(keys, i) if keys[i] == "<" else None
        i = m.end() if m else i + 1
        total += 1
    return total

guide.prereqs: The *Dot command* lesson (why keystroke counts are a useful, if crude, measure). Regular expressions anchored at a position (`pattern.match(s, i)`).
guide.intuition: It is a tokeniser with exactly two token shapes: a recognised `<…>` group, or one character. The work is in being strict about what counts as a recognised group so that literal `<` characters in the keystrokes are not swallowed.
hints: Walk an index through the string; at each `<` try to match a special key *at that position*.
Build the pattern from an alternation of names, an optional run of modifier prefixes, and `re.I`.
If the match fails, consume one character and add one to the score, exactly as for any other key.
guide.brute_force: `len(keys)` overcounts every special key, and the lazy pattern `<[^<>]+>` undercounts whenever the text contains an innocent `<…>` such as an HTML tag being typed. Both are tempting and wrong.
guide.approach:
Compile one regular expression for special keys and chords. Loop: if the current character is `<` and the pattern matches here, jump to the end of the match; otherwise advance by one. Add 1 each time.

**Dry run** `A;<Esc>j.`: `A` (1), `;` (2), `<Esc>` matches (3), `j` (4), `.` (5).
guide.pitfalls:
- Case sensitivity: `<esc>` and `<ESC>` are the same key.
- Stacked modifiers such as `<C-S-Tab>`.
- `<F123>` is not a function key: it is six ordinary keys.
- `<C->>` is Ctrl plus the character `>`.
guide.follow_up: Weight the score: charge 2 for chords and for upper-case letters (they need a modifier), then compare `A` with `$a`.

vim-dot-plan.title: Dot plan versus substitute: who wins?
vim-dot-plan.description:
You need to rename the identifier `old` to `new` everywhere in `text`. Two plans are on the table.

**Plan A, the dot formula.** Search for the whole word, change the first match, then alternate `n` (next match)
and `.` (repeat the change):

```
/\<old\><CR>   cw new <Esc>   n.   n.   ...
```

**Plan B, one substitute command:**

```
:%s/\<old\>/new/g<CR>
```

Let `k` be the number of **whole-word** occurrences of `old` in `text`: occurrences that are neither preceded
nor followed by a keyword character (`A-Za-z0-9_`). `old` and `new` consist only of keyword characters and
`text` may span several lines. Every key costs 1, and `<CR>` and `<Esc>` are one key each, so

- Plan A costs `(len(old) + 6) + (len(new) + 3) + 2 * (k - 1)`
- Plan B costs `len(old) + len(new) + 12`

Write `dotPlan(text, old, new)` returning `[dots, cost_a, cost_b]`, where `dots = k - 1` is how many times `.` is
pressed. If `k` is 0 return `[0, 0, 0]`: there is nothing to do.

**Example:** `text = "n = 1\nprint(n, n2)"`, `old = "n"`, `new = "count"` → `[1, 17, 18]` (two matches; `n2` and `print` do not count)

**Example:** `text = "id id id id"`, `old = "id"`, `new = "key"` → `[3, 20, 17]`
vim-dot-plan.starter:
def dotPlan(text: str, old: str, new: str) -> List[int]:
    pass
vim-dot-plan.solution:
import re

def dotPlan(text, old, new):
    k = len(re.findall(r"(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])" + re.escape(old) + r"(?![A-Za-z0-9_])", text))
    if k == 0:
        return [0, 0, 0]
    dot_total = (len(old) + 6) + (len(new) + 3) + 2 * (k - 1)
    sub_total = len(old) + len(new) + 12
    return [k - 1, dot_total, sub_total]

guide.prereqs: The *Dot formula* lesson and the *Substitution* lesson. Word boundaries in regular expressions.
guide.intuition: Both costs are fixed formulas; the only computation is counting whole-word matches, which is what Vim's `\<` and `\>` anchors do. Subtract the formulas and the lengths cancel: Plan A wins only when `2k + 7 < 12`, that is for one or two matches. The dot formula earns its keep through *control* (you can skip a match), not through raw key count on big jobs.
hints: A whole-word match is `old` with no keyword character immediately before or after it.
Use look-arounds: `(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])` and `(?![A-Za-z0-9_])`.
Handle `k == 0` before applying the formulas, otherwise `dots` becomes -1.
guide.brute_force: Scan every index, compare the slice with `old`, and test the neighbours by hand. O(n·m), fine for these sizes.
guide.approach:
Count with one regular expression, then plug into the formulas.

**Dry run** `n = 1\nprint(n, n2)` with `n` → `count`: matches at the first `n` and inside the call; the `n` of `print` is preceded by `i`, the `n` of `n2` is followed by `2`. k = 2, dots = 1, A = 7 + 8 + 2 = 17, B = 1 + 5 + 12 = 18.
guide.pitfalls:
- `text.count(old)` counts substrings such as the `n` in `print`.
- Splitting on whitespace misses `(user)` and `user.id`.
- The underscore is a keyword character: `user_id` does not contain the word `user`.
- Zero matches.
guide.follow_up: Add Plan C: `*` on the first occurrence instead of typing the search (cost 1 instead of `len(old) + 6`). When does it beat Plan B?

vim-normal-sim.title: A tiny Normal-mode simulator
vim-normal-sim.description:
Simulate a small subset of Normal mode on a buffer. `lines` is a non-empty list of strings; the cursor starts at
row 0, column 0; there is a single register, initially empty. Return `[lines, row, col]` after running `keys`.

"Clamp" means `col = max(0, min(col, len(current_line) - 1))`. "First non-blank" means the index of the first
character that is not a space or tab, or 0 if there is none.

| key | effect |
|---|---|
| `h` `l` | column − 1 / + 1, clamped |
| `j` `k` | row + 1 / − 1 if that row exists, then clamp the column to the new line |
| `0` `$` | first column / last column of the line |
| `x` | on a non-empty line: delete the character under the cursor into the register (**character-wise**), then clamp |
| `dd` | delete the current line into the register (**line-wise**). A buffer never becomes empty: deleting the only line leaves `[""]`. Row is clamped to the last line; column = first non-blank |
| `yy` | copy the current line into the register (line-wise); cursor unchanged |
| `p` | put after. Line-wise register: insert it as a new line **below**, move to it, column = first non-blank. Character-wise: insert the text right after the cursor character (at column 0 on an empty line); cursor on the last inserted character |
| `P` | put before. Line-wise: insert as a new line **above**; the cursor is on the new line, column = first non-blank. Character-wise: insert at the cursor column; cursor on the last inserted character |
| `J` | join the next line onto this one (no-op on the last line): strip the next line's leading blanks and concatenate with **one space**, except use no separator when the current line is empty, the current line ends in a blank, the stripped next line is empty, or the stripped next line starts with `)`. Cursor column = length of the original current line, clamped |
| `r{c}` | replace the character under the cursor with `c` (nothing on an empty line); cursor unchanged |
| `~` | toggle the case of the character under the cursor, then move one column right (clamped); nothing on an empty line |

`p`/`P` with an empty register do nothing. `keys` contains only the commands above.

**Example:** `lines = ["one", "two"]`, `keys = "ddp"` → `[["two", "one"], 1, 0]` (swap two lines)

**Example:** `lines = ["teh"]`, `keys = "lxp"` → `[["the"], 0, 2]` (swap two characters)

**Example:** `lines = ["foo(", "    a,", "    b", ")"]`, `keys = "JJJ"` → `[["foo( a, b)"], 0, 9]`
vim-normal-sim.starter:
def normalSim(lines: List[str], keys: str) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Registers* lesson (character-wise versus line-wise text), the *Normal mode grammar* lesson.
guide.intuition: The whole simulator is a loop over keys with three pieces of state: the buffer, the cursor, and one register that remembers both the text **and how it was captured**. That second fact is why `ddp` swaps lines while `xp` swaps characters although both end in the same `p`.
hints: Store the register as a pair `(text, kind)` with kind `'l'` or `'c'`.
Consume two characters for `dd`, `yy` and `r{c}`; everything else is one key.
Write `clamp` and `first_nonblank` helpers first; nearly every command ends with one of them.
guide.brute_force: A long `if` chain operating on the list of strings *is* the natural solution; there is no asymptotically different approach. The risk is not speed but subtle cursor rules.
guide.approach:
Process keys left to right, applying the table.

**Dry run** `["teh"]` with `lxp`: `l` → col 1. `x` removes `e`: line `th`, register (`e`, char), col clamped to 1. `p` inserts after column 1 at index 2: `the`, cursor on the inserted character, col 2.
guide.complexity: O(len(keys) × L) where L is the line length (each edit rebuilds a string), plus O(rows) for line insertions and deletions.
guide.pitfalls:
- Line-wise `P` keeps the same row index (the new line now occupies it); line-wise `p` increments it.
- Character-wise `p` on an empty line inserts at column 0, not 1.
- `dd` on the last remaining line must leave one empty line.
- `J` strips the *next* line's leading blanks and can decide to insert no space at all.
- After `x` at the end of a line the cursor steps back.
guide.follow_up: Add counts (`3dd`, `2p`), `u` for undo using a stack of buffer snapshots, and `.` to repeat the last change.

vim-registers.title: Simulate the unnamed, numbered and named registers
vim-registers.description:
Model how yanks and deletes flow through Vim's registers. `ops` is a list of `[kind, name, text]`:

- `kind` is `"y"` (yank) or `"d"` (delete or change);
- `name` is the register given with a `"x` prefix, or `""` when the command had no prefix;
- `text` is what was captured. A text **containing a newline** is a multi-line capture.

Rules of this model (they follow Vim's documented behaviour):

1. `name == "_"` (black hole): nothing at all changes.
2. No prefix, **yank**: the text goes to register `0`.
3. No prefix, **delete**, multi-line text: registers `1`…`8` shift down to `2`…`9` (the old `9` is lost) and the
   text goes to `1`.
4. No prefix, **delete**, text without a newline: the text goes to the small-delete register `-`. The numbered
   registers are untouched.
5. Lower-case name `a`–`z`: that register is overwritten. Registers `0`–`9` and `-` are untouched.
6. Upper-case name `A`–`Z`: the text is **appended** to the lower-case register of the same letter (plain
   concatenation).
7. In every case except the black hole, the unnamed register `"` ends up holding what the written register now
   holds (for an append, the whole accumulated text).

Then answer `queries`, a list of register names among `"`, `0`–`9`, `-`, `a`–`z`: return each one's contents,
with `""` for a register that was never set.

**Example:** `ops = [["y","","alpha"], ["d","","x"], ["d","","line\n"]]`, `queries = ['"', "0", "1", "-"]`
→ `["line\n", "alpha", "line\n", "x"]`

**Example:** `ops = [["y","a","one "], ["y","A","two"], ["d","_","junk"]]`, `queries = ["a", '"', "0"]`
→ `["one two", "one two", ""]`
vim-registers.starter:
def registerSim(ops: List[List[str]], queries: List[str]) -> List[str]:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Registers* lesson. Dictionaries.
guide.intuition: Think of the registers as a small key-value store with routing rules. A command with no prefix is routed by *what it did*: yanks to `0`, big deletes into the `1`–`9` queue, small deletes to `-`. A command with a prefix goes exactly where you said. The unnamed register is a pointer to whichever register was written last.
hints: Use a dict from register name to text; missing keys mean empty.
Shift the numbered registers from 9 down to 2, otherwise you copy one value into all of them.
After every write, set `reg['"']` to the current content of the register you just wrote.
guide.brute_force: Keep a Python list for registers 1–9 and insert at the front, truncating to nine items. That is equally fast and arguably clearer; the dict version just keeps all registers uniform.
guide.approach:
Loop over the operations, applying the first rule that matches.

**Dry run** of example 1: yank `alpha` → `0 = alpha`, `" = alpha`. Delete `x` (no newline) → `- = x`, `" = x`. Delete `line
` → nothing to shift, `1 = line
`, `" = line
`. Register `0` still holds `alpha`: that is the yank register surviving two deletes.
guide.complexity: O(len(ops) + len(queries)) time (the shift is a constant nine steps), O(total text) space.
guide.pitfalls:
- Sending every delete to register 1; small deletes go to `-`.
- Shifting upward (2 ← 1, 3 ← 2 …) copies register 1 everywhere.
- A named yank does not touch register 0.
- After an append, the unnamed register holds the whole accumulated text, not just the new piece.
- The black hole really changes nothing, not even the unnamed register.
guide.follow_up: Add the read-only registers (`.` last inserted text, `:` last Ex command, `%` file name) and the system clipboard registers `+` and `*`.

vim-macro-expand.title: Expand macros with counts
vim-macro-expand.description:
A macro is just a register full of keystrokes; `@a` types the contents of register `a`, and `7@a` does so seven
times. Macros may invoke other macros. Flatten a keystroke string into the keys that are finally executed.

`registers` maps lower-case letters to keystroke strings. Scan `keys` left to right:

- **Count.** A count is a run of digits whose first digit is `1`–`9`. (A `0` that does not continue a count is the
  "go to column 0" motion and is copied like any other key.)
- **Invocation.** An optional count followed by `@` and a lower-case letter `x` runs register `x` that many times
  (once without a count). Each run is itself expanded by these same rules. A register missing from `registers`
  is empty.
- **Repeat.** `@@` (optionally with a count) runs the register that was executed **most recently at that moment**,
  including registers run from inside other macros. If no macro has run yet it produces nothing.
- **Everything else** is copied to the output unchanged, including a count that is not followed by an invocation
  (`3j` stays `3j`).

Inputs are guaranteed not to recurse forever, and `@` is only ever used as described.

Write `expandMacro(registers, keys)` returning the flattened string.

**Example:** `registers = {"a": "A;j"}`, `keys = "3@a"` → `"A;jA;jA;j"`

**Example:** `registers = {"a": "0f,2@bj", "b": "x"}`, `keys = "@a@@"` → `"0f,xxjx"` (the most recently run register is `b`)

**Example:** `registers = {}`, `keys = "10j@q@@dd"` → `"10jdd"`
vim-macro-expand.starter:
def expandMacro(registers: Dict[str, str], keys: str) -> str:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Macros* lesson. Recursion; a simple hand-written scanner.
guide.intuition: Executing a macro is the same as typing its contents, so expansion is recursive substitution. The one piece of global state is *which register ran last*, because `@@` refers to it, and that can change while a macro is in the middle of running.
hints: Write a recursive `run(s)` that appends to a shared output list.
Read digits first; only if the next two characters form `@x` or `@@` is it a count. Otherwise emit the digits literally.
Update the last-run register *before* each recursive call, and resolve `@@` at the moment it is reached.
guide.brute_force: Repeatedly apply a regular-expression substitution replacing `N@x` by N copies of the register until nothing changes. This handles nesting, but it cannot resolve `@@` correctly because that depends on execution order.
guide.approach:
A scanner with one-token look-ahead plus recursion.

**Dry run** `@a@@` with `a = 0f,2@bj`, `b = x`: `@a` → last = a, run `0f,2@bj`: emit `0`, `f`, `,`; `2@b` → last = b, emit `x` twice; emit `j`. Back at the top level, `@@` → last is `b` → emit `x`. Output `0f,xxjx`.
guide.complexity: O(size of the output) time and space.
guide.pitfalls:
- Treating a leading `0` as a count: `0@a` is the motion `0` followed by `@a`.
- Dropping counts that belong to ordinary commands (`3j`).
- Resolving `@@` to the register named at the top level rather than the one that actually ran last.
- `@@` before any macro has run is a no-op.
guide.follow_up: Model macro abort: add a per-key predicate that can fail, and stop the *entire* remaining count when it does. That is how `100@a` stops by itself at the end of a file.

vim-ex-range.title: Parse an Ex range
vim-ex-range.description:
Most Ex commands accept a range in front: `:3,7d`, `:.,+3>`, `:'<,'>normal .`, `:%s/a/b/`. Resolve a range
specification to a pair of 1-based line numbers.

Arguments: `spec` (the range text, no spaces), `cur` (the cursor's line), `last` (the number of lines in the
buffer, at least 1) and `marks` (a dict from mark name, one character such as `a`, `<` or `>`, to a line number).

Grammar of this subset:

- `spec` is `""`, `"%"`, one *address*, or two addresses separated by a comma.
- An **address** is an optional *base* followed by zero or more *offsets*.
  - Base: a decimal number, `.` (current line), `$` (last line), or `'x` (line of mark `x`).
    A missing base means the current line, so `+2` is `.+2` and the empty string is `.`.
  - Offset: `+N` or `-N`; a bare `+` or `-` means 1. Offsets accumulate: `.+3-1` is `cur + 2`.
- In `a,b` **both** addresses are resolved relative to the cursor (that is what the comma means in Vim; the
  semicolon form is not part of this problem).
- `%` is shorthand for `1,$`.
- One address alone gives a one-line range `[n, n]`; the empty spec gives `[cur, cur]`.

Return `[start, end]`. If the two addresses come out reversed, swap them. Return `[-1, -1]` when the spec uses
an unknown mark, has a malformed address (anything that is not a valid base or offset, or more than one comma),
or when either address falls outside `1..last`.

**Example:** `spec = ".,+3"`, `cur = 5`, `last = 20`, `marks = {}` → `[5, 8]`

**Example:** `spec = "'<,'>"`, `cur = 9`, `last = 20`, `marks = {"<": 4, ">": 9}` → `[4, 9]`

**Example:** `spec = "%"`, `cur = 2`, `last = 12` → `[1, 12]`
vim-ex-range.starter:
def parseRange(spec: str, cur: int, last: int, marks: Dict[str, int]) -> List[int]:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Command-line mode* lesson (ranges and addresses). Writing a small recursive-descent style scanner.
guide.intuition: A range is at most two addresses, and an address is a starting line plus a running sum of signed offsets. Parse the base, then loop over offsets. Everything else is validation.
hints: Handle `%` up front; then `spec.split(',')` gives one or two address strings (the empty string is a valid address).
In the address parser, decide the base from the first character, then consume `+`/`-` followed by optional digits until the string ends.
Return `None` from the address parser for anything unexpected, and turn it into `[-1, -1]` at the top level.
guide.brute_force: A single regular expression such as `^(base)?((?:[+-]\d*)*)$` per address also works; you still need a loop (or `re.findall`) to add up the offsets.
guide.approach:
`addr(s)` → integer or `None`. Top level: `%`, else split on the comma, resolve, validate bounds, order.

**Dry run** `2,$-1` with last = 20: first address has base 2, no offsets → 2. Second: base `$` = 20, offset `-1` → 19. Both within 1..20 → `[2, 19]`.
guide.pitfalls:
- Resolving the second address relative to the first: that is `;`, not `,`.
- A bare `+` means +1, not +0.
- `0` is a number but not a valid line in this model.
- The empty string on either side of the comma is legal and means the current line.
- Forgetting to swap a backwards range.
guide.follow_up: Add pattern addresses (`/re/` and `?re?`), the `;` separator, and `:{range}` with a count such as `:d 3`.

vim-substitute.title: Apply :s to a range of lines
vim-substitute.description:
Implement the heart of `:[range]s/{pattern}/{replacement}/[flags]`.

Arguments: `lines` (the buffer), `start` and `end` (a valid 1-based inclusive range), `pat`, `rep`, `flags`.

- `pat` uses **Python `re` syntax** so that you can concentrate on substitute semantics rather than on Vim's
  regex dialect. It never matches the empty string.
- Without the `g` flag only the **first** match on each line is replaced. With `g`, every non-overlapping match.
- Flag `i` makes matching case-insensitive.
- Flag `n` only counts: the buffer is returned unchanged, but the counts are reported as if the substitution ran.
- In `rep`:
  - `&` and `\0` stand for the whole match;
  - `\1` … `\9` stand for the corresponding capture group (the empty string if that group did not participate
    or does not exist);
  - `\t` is a tab character;
  - a backslash followed by any other character yields that character literally (so `\&` is an ampersand and
    `\\` is a backslash; `\r` and `\n` do not occur in the tests);
  - everything else is literal.

Return `[new_lines, substitutions, lines_changed]`: the same two numbers Vim reports as "N substitutions on M
lines". Lines outside the range are never touched.

**Example:** `lines = ["a-b-c", "d-e"]`, range `1,2`, `pat = "-"`, `rep = "+"`, `flags = ""` → `[["a+b-c", "d+e"], 2, 2]`

**Example:** same buffer with `flags = "g"` → `[["a+b+c", "d+e"], 3, 2]`

**Example:** `lines = ["Doe, Jane"]`, `pat = r"(\w+), (\w+)"`, `rep = r"\2 \1 <&>"`, `flags = ""` → `[["Jane Doe <Doe, Jane>"], 1, 1]`
vim-substitute.starter:
def substitute(lines: List[str], start: int, end: int, pat: str, rep: str, flags: str) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Substitution* lesson. `re.compile`, `Pattern.subn` with a function as the replacement.
guide.intuition: Three independent pieces: *which lines* (the range), *which matches on a line* (first or all), and *what to write* (the replacement mini-language). Python's own replacement syntax differs from Vim's (`&` is not special in Python, `\g<0>` is), so expand the replacement yourself.
hints: `rx.subn(func, line, count=1)` replaces only the first match and tells you how many replacements were made.
Write `expand(match)` that walks `rep` character by character, handling backslash pairs and `&`.
For the `n` flag do all the counting but skip the assignment back into the list.
guide.brute_force: Find matches manually with `rx.search` in a loop, slicing and rebuilding the line each time. Correct but quadratic on long lines, and you must be careful to continue searching after the inserted text, not inside it.
guide.approach:
Compile once, loop over the range, call `subn` with the expansion function, accumulate counts.

**Dry run** `Doe, Jane` with `(\w+), (\w+)` → `\2 \1 <&>`: one match, groups `Doe` and `Jane`. Expanding: `\2` → `Jane`, space, `\1` → `Doe`, space, `<`, `&` → `Doe, Jane`, `>`.
guide.complexity: O(total length of the lines in the range × cost of matching), O(size of the output) space.
guide.pitfalls:
- Passing `rep` straight to `re.sub`: Python does not understand `&`, and `\0` means something else.
- Replacing every match when `g` is absent.
- Counting changed lines instead of substitutions (or the reverse).
- Touching lines outside the range.
- A group that did not participate is `None` in Python; Vim inserts nothing.
guide.follow_up: Add `~` (previous replacement string), `\u`/`\U…\E` case modifiers, and the `c` flag driven by a list of y/n answers.

vim-global-command.title: Run :g and :v with d, m and t
vim-global-command.description:
`:g/{pattern}/{cmd}` runs an Ex command on every line that matches a pattern; `:v/{pattern}/{cmd}` (also spelled
`:g!`) runs it on every line that does **not** match. It works in two passes:

1. **Mark** every line of the buffer for which the test holds (`re.search(pat, line)` succeeds for `:g`, fails
   for `:v`). `pat` uses Python `re` syntax.
2. **Execute** `cmd` once for each marked line, visiting them in their original top-to-bottom order, with that
   line as the current line. Lines created by the command itself are not marked.

Supported commands:

| `cmd` | Ex meaning | effect per marked line |
|---|---|---|
| `d` | delete | remove the line |
| `m0` | move to before line 1 | the line becomes the first line |
| `m$` | move to after the last line | the line becomes the last line |
| `t0` | copy to before line 1 | a copy becomes the first line |
| `t$` | copy to after the last line | a copy becomes the last line |

Arguments: `lines`, `pat`, `invert` (`False` for `:g`, `True` for `:v`), `cmd`. Return the resulting list of lines.

Think about what the per-line execution order does: `:g/^/m0` moves line 1 to the top, then line 2 above it, then
line 3 above that … and so reverses the buffer.

**Example:** `lines = ["a", "# x", "b", "# y"]`, `pat = "^#"`, `invert = False`, `cmd = "d"` → `["a", "b"]`

**Example:** `lines = ["1", "2", "3"]`, `pat = "^"`, `invert = False`, `cmd = "m0"` → `["3", "2", "1"]`

**Example:** `lines = ["x", "TODO a", "y", "TODO b"]`, `pat = "TODO"`, `invert = False`, `cmd = "t$"` → `["x", "TODO a", "y", "TODO b", "TODO a", "TODO b"]`
vim-global-command.starter:
def globalCmd(lines: List[str], pat: str, invert: bool, cmd: str) -> List[str]:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Global command* lesson. `re.search`; list comprehensions.
guide.intuition: Because the marking pass is finished before anything runs, you can reason about the final layout directly: split the buffer into *marked* and *unmarked* lines. Deleting keeps the unmarked ones; moving or copying to the end appends the marked ones in order; moving or copying to the top prepends them **reversed**, because each later line lands above the earlier ones.
hints: Compute a boolean per line first; XOR it with `invert`.
Build two lists, `marked` and `rest`, preserving order.
For `m0` and `t0`, reverse `marked` before prepending.
guide.brute_force: Simulate literally: keep a list of (line, mark) pairs and for each originally marked line locate it, remove or copy it, and reinsert. O(n²) because each move shifts the list, and matching while you mutate (a single pass) is wrong: moved lines get tested again.
guide.approach:
Mark, partition, assemble.

**Dry run** `["1","2","3"]`, `:g/^/m0`: all three are marked. Executing in order: `1` moves to the top (no change), `2` moves above it → `2,1,3`, `3` moves above → `3,2,1`. The formula gives `marked[::-1] + rest` = `[3,2,1] + []`.
guide.complexity: O(n × match cost) time, O(n) space.
guide.pitfalls:
- Testing lines while mutating: `:g` marks first, so copies appended by `t$` are never re-examined.
- Forgetting that `m0`/`t0` reverse the order.
- Using `fullmatch`: `:g/abc/` matches anywhere in the line.
- Ignoring `invert`.
guide.follow_up: Support `:g/pat/normal {keys}` by plugging in the simulator from `vim-normal-sim`, and `:g/pat/s/a/b/g` using `vim-substitute`.

vim-very-magic.title: Translate a very magic pattern to Python
vim-very-magic.description:
With the `\v` switch ("very magic"), Vim patterns read almost like Perl or Python regular expressions: every
ASCII character except letters, digits and underscore is special unless escaped. *Almost*. Translate a
very-magic pattern into an equivalent Python `re` pattern for the following subset.

A leading `\v` in the input, if present, is dropped. Then scan left to right and apply the **first** rule that fits:

| in the Vim pattern | emit | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `\a` `\l` `\u` `\h` `\x` | `[A-Za-z]` `[a-z]` `[A-Z]` `[A-Za-z_]` `[0-9A-Fa-f]` | Vim-only character classes |
| `\` + any other letter or digit (`\d`, `\w`, `\s`, `\D`, `\t`, `\n`, …) | unchanged | same in both dialects |
| `\` + one of `. ^ $ * + ? ( ) [ ] { } \| \` | unchanged (still escaped) | a literal that Python must also escape |
| `\` + any other character (`\<`, `\>`, `\=`, `\/`, `\%`, …) | just that character | a literal that needs no escape in Python |
| `<` or `>` | `\b` | word boundary |
| `=` | `?` | optional (Vim's alias for `?`) |
| `%(` | `(?:` | non-capturing group |
| `{-}` | `*?` | as few as possible |
| `{-N}`, `{-N,}`, `{-N,M}`, `{-,M}` | `{N}?`, `{N,}?`, `{N,M}?`, `{,M}?` | lazy counted repeat |
| `[` … `]` | copied verbatim | a bracket expression: an optional `^` and then an optional `]` right after the `[` are part of it, a backslash protects the next character, and it ends at the next `]` |
| anything else | unchanged | `( ) \| + ? * . ^ $ {n,m}` and literals mean the same |

Inputs are well formed and never contain unescaped `@`, `~` or `&`.

Write `veryMagicToPython(pat)` returning the Python pattern string.

**Example:** `\v<(get|set)_\a+>` → `\b(get|set)_[A-Za-z]+\b`

**Example:** `\v#\x{6}` → `#[0-9A-Fa-f]{6}`

**Example:** `\vhttps=://%(www\.)=[^/ ]+` → `https?://(?:www\.)?[^/ ]+`

guide.prereqs: The *Patterns and search* lesson (magic levels). Comfortable reading Python regular expressions.
guide.intuition: Very magic is already 90% Python syntax, so this is a pass-through scanner with a handful of rewrites. What makes it a scanner rather than a chain of `str.replace` calls is *context*: a `<` inside `[...]` or after a backslash must not become `\b`.
hints: Process the string with an index, not with global replacements; decide what to do from the current character (and sometimes the next).
Deal with the backslash case first: it consumes two characters and has four sub-cases.
Copy a bracket expression in one go. Find its end carefully: `[]x]` and `[^]x]` contain a literal `]`.
guide.brute_force: A sequence of `replace` calls handles the three examples but fails as soon as a rewritten character appears escaped or inside a bracket expression, e.g. `[<>=]` or `\<`.
guide.approach:
Loop with `i`; branch on backslash, `<`/`>`, `=`, `%(`, `{-`, `[`, default.

**Dry run** `https=://%(www\.)=[^/ ]+`: `https` copied; `=` → `?`; `://` copied; `%(` → `(?:`; `www` copied; `\.` stays `\.`; `)` copied; `=` → `?`; `[^/ ]` copied verbatim; `+` copied.
guide.pitfalls:
- Global replacement of `=` or `<` corrupts bracket expressions and escaped literals.
- `\<` in very magic is a *literal* less-than sign, the opposite of its meaning in the default magic mode.
- `{-}` is `*?`, but `{-1,}` is `{1,}?` (that is, `+?`).
- `\x` is a class in Vim but the start of a hex escape in Python.
guide.follow_up: Go the other way for *magic* (the default) patterns, where `(`, `|`, `+`, `?`, `{` need a backslash to be special, and translate look-arounds (`@=`, `@!`, `@<=`).

vim-jump-list.title: Navigate the jump list
vim-jump-list.description:
Vim records where you were before each *jump* (`G`, `/search`, `%`, a mark…) so that `Ctrl-O` can take you back
and `Ctrl-I` forward again. Model one window whose positions are plain line numbers.

State: the cursor line `cur` (initially `1`), a list `L` (initially empty) and an index `idx` into it.
`idx == len(L)` means "past the newest entry", which is where you are after any ordinary jump.

| op | effect |
|---|---|
| `["jump", n]` | record where you are, then go: remove every entry equal to `cur` from `L`, append `cur`, set `idx = len(L)`, then `cur = n` |
| `["back"]` (`Ctrl-O`) | if `idx == len(L)`, first record the current position so you can return to it: remove entries equal to `cur`, append `cur`, set `idx = len(L) - 1`. Then, if `idx > 0`: `idx -= 1` and `cur = L[idx]`; otherwise nothing more happens |
| `["fwd"]` (`Ctrl-I`) | if `idx < len(L) - 1`: `idx += 1` and `cur = L[idx]`; otherwise nothing happens |

Two consequences worth noticing: the list never holds the same line twice (the older duplicate is dropped), and
a jump made from the middle of the list does **not** discard the newer entries, unlike a browser's history.

Write `jumpList(ops)` returning `[cur, L]`.

**Example:** `[["jump", 40], ["jump", 90], ["back"]]` → `[40, [1, 40, 90]]`

**Example:** `[["jump", 40], ["jump", 90], ["back"], ["back"], ["fwd"]]` → `[40, [1, 40, 90]]`

**Example:** `[["jump", 40], ["jump", 90], ["back"], ["jump", 7]]` → `[7, [1, 90, 40]]`

guide.prereqs: The *Jumps* lesson. Lists and an index pointer; the browser-history design problem is a useful contrast.
guide.intuition: The list stores *departure points*. A jump pushes the place you are leaving. The first `Ctrl-O` must also push the place you are leaving, otherwise `Ctrl-I` could never bring you back to it. De-duplication keeps the list a set of distinct places ordered by how recently you left them.
hints: Track three variables exactly as the statement names them: `cur`, `L`, `idx`.
Write the de-duplicate-and-append step once; both `jump` and the first `back` use it.
After the special first-`back` step, `idx` points at the entry for the current position, so a single `idx -= 1` moves to the previous place.
guide.brute_force: There is no cheaper trick than simulating; a naive version simply uses list filtering for the de-duplication, which is O(len(L)) per jump and entirely adequate (Vim caps the list at 100).
guide.approach:
Simulate each operation.

**Dry run** of example 3: jump 40 → L = [1], cur 40. jump 90 → L = [1, 40], cur 90, idx 2. back → idx equals len, so record 90: L = [1, 40, 90], idx 2 → 1, cur 40. jump 7 → remove 40, append 40: L = [1, 90, 40], idx 3, cur 7.
guide.pitfalls:
- Truncating the forward entries on a new jump, as a browser would.
- Forgetting to record the current position on the first `back`; then `fwd` cannot return.
- Keeping duplicates, which makes `Ctrl-O` appear to do nothing.
- `fwd` stops at the last entry, index `len(L) - 1`, not at `len(L)`.
guide.follow_up: Positions in real Vim are (file, line, column); extend the model with file names so that `Ctrl-O` can cross buffers, and cap the list at 100 entries.

vim-change-list.title: Walk the change list with g; and g,
vim-change-list.description:
Separately from the jump list, each buffer remembers **where its text was changed**. `g;` travels back to older
changes and `g,` forward to newer ones. Model it with line numbers only.

State: cursor line `cur` (initially `1`), list `L` of changed lines (initially empty), index `idx` (initially `0`).

| op | effect |
|---|---|
| `["move", n]` | `cur = n`. Nothing is recorded: plain movement is not a change |
| `["edit", n]` | make a change on line `n`: `cur = n`; append `n` to `L` unless the newest entry is already `n` (consecutive changes on one line are merged); keep at most the newest 100 entries; then `idx = len(L)` (past the newest entry) |
| `["g;"]` | if `idx > 0`: `idx -= 1` and `cur = L[idx]`. Otherwise the command fails and the cursor stays |
| `["g,"]` | if `idx < len(L) - 1`: `idx += 1` and `cur = L[idx]`. Otherwise it fails and the cursor stays |

Return a list with the cursor line **after each `g;` or `g,`** (failed ones included), in order.

**Example:** `[["edit", 12], ["edit", 30], ["move", 99], ["g;"], ["g;"], ["g;"], ["g,"]]` → `[30, 12, 12, 30]`

**Example:** `[["edit", 5], ["edit", 5], ["edit", 8], ["g;"], ["g;"]]` → `[8, 5]`

guide.prereqs: The *Jumps* lesson (change list section).
guide.intuition: It is a history list with a cursor into it, simpler than the jump list: only edits append, navigation never modifies the list, and any new edit resets the index to just past the end.
hints: Keep `idx == len(L)` after every edit, so the first `g;` lands on the newest change.
Merging means: compare with `L[-1]` before appending.
Append to the output after *every* `g;`/`g,`, even when the index did not move.
guide.brute_force: Direct simulation is already optimal; the only inefficiency to avoid is `pop(0)` on a huge list, which the 100-entry cap makes irrelevant (use `collections.deque(maxlen=100)` if you prefer).
guide.approach:
One loop, four cases.

**Dry run** of example 1: edits give L = [12, 30], idx 2. `move 99` changes only the cursor. `g;` → idx 1, cur 30. `g;` → idx 0, cur 12. `g;` → idx is 0: fails, cur stays 12. `g,` → idx 1, cur 30.
guide.pitfalls:
- Recording plain movement.
- Starting the index *on* the newest entry: then the first `g;` skips it.
- Letting `g,` step to `len(L)`, which is not an entry.
- Forgetting the cap: with 150 edits the oldest reachable change is line 51.
guide.follow_up: Add the `'.` mark (line of the last change) and `gi` (resume inserting where Insert mode was last stopped), both of which read from the same bookkeeping.

vim-buffer-list.title: Buffer list and the alternate file
vim-buffer-list.description:
Simulate the buffer list of one Vim window. State: the current buffer name `cur` (initially `""`, meaning no
file), the **alternate** buffer `alt` (initially `""`; this is what `#` and `Ctrl-^` refer to) and the ordered
list `L` of listed buffers (initially empty).

| op | Ex command | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `["e", name]` | `:edit name` | if `name == cur`, nothing. Otherwise append `name` to `L` unless already listed; if `cur` is not `""` set `alt = cur`; then `cur = name` |
| `["bn"]` | `:bnext` | if `L` has more than one buffer: `alt = cur`, and `cur` becomes the buffer after it in `L`, wrapping from the last to the first. Otherwise nothing |
| `["bp"]` | `:bprevious` | the same in the other direction, wrapping from the first to the last |
| `["alt"]` | `Ctrl-^` or `:b#` | if `alt` is not `""`, swap `cur` and `alt`. Otherwise nothing |
| `["bd"]` | `:bdelete` | if `cur` is `""`, nothing. Otherwise remove `cur` from `L` (remember its index `i`). The new current buffer is `alt` if `alt` is not `""`; else the buffer now at index `i` of `L`; else, if the deleted buffer was last, the new last buffer; else `""` when `L` is empty. In all cases `alt` becomes `""` |

Write `bufferSim(ops)` returning `[cur, alt, L]`.

**Example:** `[["e","a.py"], ["e","b.py"], ["e","c.py"], ["alt"]]` → `["b.py", "c.py", ["a.py","b.py","c.py"]]`

**Example:** `[["e","a.py"], ["e","b.py"], ["e","c.py"], ["bn"], ["bn"]]` → `["b.py", "a.py", ["a.py","b.py","c.py"]]`

**Example:** `[["e","a.py"], ["e","b.py"], ["bd"], ["bd"]]` → `["", "", []]`

guide.prereqs: The *Buffers and the argument list* lesson.
guide.intuition: Two names and a list. Every command that switches buffers demotes the old current buffer to *alternate*; `Ctrl-^` simply swaps the two names. Deleting is the only fiddly part because a replacement has to be chosen.
hints: Treat the empty string as 'no buffer' consistently for both `cur` and `alt`.
`(i + step) % len(L)` gives wrap-around in both directions.
For `bd`, record the index before popping; after popping, that same index is the buffer that used to follow.
guide.brute_force: Simulation is the solution. Using `list.index` makes each step O(len(L)); keeping a position dict would make it O(1) but is not worth the bookkeeping at this size.
guide.approach:
Dispatch on the op.

**Dry run** of example 2: after three edits cur = c.py, alt = b.py. `bn` wraps: alt = c.py, cur = a.py. `bn`: alt = a.py, cur = b.py. Result `[b.py, a.py, …]`.
guide.pitfalls:
- Setting `alt` when re-editing the current buffer (it must not become its own alternate).
- Forgetting that `:bnext` also updates the alternate.
- Off-by-one choosing the successor after deleting the last entry.
- `Ctrl-^` with no alternate is an error, not a jump to the first buffer.
guide.follow_up: Add `:b N` by buffer number (numbers are never reused), hidden-and-modified buffers that refuse `:bdelete` without `!`, and the argument list as a separate, user-curated subset.

vim-visual-block-insert.title: Visual-block insert and append
vim-visual-block-insert.description:
In Visual-block mode (`Ctrl-V`) you select a rectangle, and `I` or `A` then types the same text on every row of
it. Reproduce the three common cases on rows `top..bottom` (0-based, inclusive):

| `mode` | keys in Vim | effect on each row of the block |
|---|---|---|
| `"I"` | `Ctrl-V` … `I text Esc` | insert `text` **before** column `col` (the block's left edge). Rows too short to have a character at `col` (`len(row) <= col`) are **left alone** |
| `"A"` | `Ctrl-V` … `A text Esc` | append `text` **after** column `col` (the block's right edge). Rows too short are first **padded with spaces** up to and including column `col` |
| `"$A"` | `Ctrl-V` … `$A text Esc` | the block extends to the end of every row: append `text` at the end of each row, whatever its length (`col` is ignored) |

Rows outside `top..bottom` are untouched. Return the new list of lines.

**Example:** `lines = ["alpha", "beta", "gamma"]`, rows `0..2`, `col = 0`, `mode = "I"`, `text = "- "` → `["- alpha", "- beta", "- gamma"]`

**Example:** `lines = ["x = 1", "yy = 22", "z"]`, rows `0..2`, `mode = "$A"`, `text = ";"` → `["x = 1;", "yy = 22;", "z;"]`

**Example:** `lines = ["abcdef", "ab", "abcd"]`, rows `0..2`, `col = 3`, `mode = "A"`, `text = "|"` → `["abcd|ef", "ab  |", "abcd|"]`
vim-visual-block-insert.starter:
def blockEdit(lines: List[str], top: int, bottom: int, col: int, mode: str, text: str) -> List[str]:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The *Visual mode* lesson (Visual-block). String slicing.
guide.intuition: A block edit is the same single-line edit applied to each row; the three modes differ only in **where** on the row the text goes and in **how short rows are treated**: skipped by `I`, padded by `A`, irrelevant for `$A`.
hints: Copy the list first so that rows outside the block stay as they are.
`I` inserts at index `col`; `A` inserts at index `col + 1`.
For `A` on a short row, pad to length `col + 1` before slicing.
guide.brute_force: Convert every row to a list of characters and insert character by character. It is equivalent and only slower by a constant factor.
guide.approach:
Loop over the rows in the block and splice.

**Dry run** `["abcdef", "ab", "abcd"]`, col 3, `A`, `|`: row 0 → `abcd` + `|` + `ef`. Row 1 has length 2 ≤ 3: pad to `ab` + two spaces (length 4), then append → `ab  |`. Row 2 → `abcd|`.
guide.complexity: O(total length of the rows in the block) time and space.
guide.pitfalls:
- Applying `I` to short rows: Python slicing would silently append the text at their end.
- Padding one space too few or too many for `A`.
- Confusing `A` (rectangular, pads) with `$A` (ragged right edge, never pads).
- Editing rows outside the block.
guide.follow_up: Add `c` (replace the block's columns `col..col2` on each row with the text) and `r{char}` (overwrite every character of the block).
